items.title: Estimating kidney function for dosing
items.subtitle: Cockcroft-Gault, eGFR, weights and unstable kidney function
items.summary: Most drug labels and dose tables use Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance. Choose the right weight, and be cautious when creatinine is changing, because the estimate then lags behind true function.

sections.title: Cockcroft-Gault
sections.text:
• CrCl (mL/min) = (140 minus age) x weight in kg / (72 x serum creatinine in mg/dL).
• Multiply by 0.85 for women.
• With creatinine in micromol/L: CrCl = (140 minus age) x weight x 1.23 (men) or 1.04 (women) / creatinine.
• Product labels and most antibiotic dosing tables use this estimate.

sections.title: eGFR (CKD-EPI)
sections.text:
• eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m2 of body surface area.
• For very large or very small patients, convert to mL/min: eGFR x (patient BSA / 1.73).
• Cystatin C-based estimates help when muscle mass is abnormal (sarcopenia, amputation, cirrhosis, very high muscle mass), where available.

sections.title: Which weight to use
sections.text:
• Ideal body weight (IBW): men 50 kg + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 feet; women 45.5 kg + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 feet.
• Adjusted body weight = IBW + 0.4 x (actual weight minus IBW).
• Common approach: use actual weight if it is below ideal; ideal weight if the patient is at normal weight; adjusted weight if actual weight is more than about 120% of ideal.
• Follow your hospital pharmacy policy, because conventions differ.

sections.title: Unstable kidney function
sections.text:
• In acute kidney injury or sepsis, creatinine lags behind true GFR: estimates are unreliable.
• In the first 24 to 48 hours of sepsis, give full loading and first doses of beta-lactams and other time-critical antibiotics, because underdosing early carries more risk than a short period of higher exposure.
• Reassess renal function daily, and adjust doses as it settles.
• Rising creatinine may overestimate recovery; falling creatinine may underestimate it.

sections.title: Augmented renal clearance
sections.text:
• CrCl of about 130 mL/min or more, seen in young patients with sepsis, burns, trauma, brain injury, and after major surgery.
• Standard doses of renally cleared drugs (beta-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides) may be too low.
• Consider higher doses, shorter intervals, extended or continuous infusions, and therapeutic drug monitoring.
• Measured urinary creatinine clearance over 8 to 24 hours can confirm it.

sections.title: Pitfalls
sections.text:
• Trimethoprim, cimetidine and some other drugs raise creatinine without a true GFR fall.
• Elderly, malnourished and cirrhotic patients may have normal creatinine with low GFR.
• Check the product label or local table for each drug, and recheck doses within 48 to 72 hours of any change in kidney function.
• Report the renal function used on the prescription.

items.source: Cockcroft-Gault equation, KDIGO guidance, SCCM/ASHP critical care dosing guidance. Verify against your hospital pharmacy policy.

items.title: Renal dose bands by antibiotic
items.subtitle: Adults | CrCl in mL/min, based on usual doses
items.summary: A quick reference for common antibiotics: beta-lactams, carbapenems, quinolones, folate antagonists, glycopeptides, aminoglycosides and others. Bands assume the usual dose shown; always check the product label and your local table.

sections.title: Beta-lactams
sections.text:
• Ampicillin IV: CrCl above 50: every 6 hours; 10 to 50: every 6 to 12 hours; below 10: every 12 to 24 hours.
• Amoxicillin oral: CrCl 10 to 30: 250 to 500 mg every 12 hours; below 10: every 24 hours; avoid the 875 mg tablet when CrCl is below 30.
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate oral: CrCl below 30: 500/125 mg every 12 hours, with no 875 mg tablets; below 10: every 24 hours.
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g: CrCl 30 or above: every 6 to 8 hours; 15 to 29: every 12 hours; 5 to 14: every 24 hours.
• Penicillin G: CrCl 10 to 50: about 75% of the dose; below 10: 20 to 50%.
• Piperacillin-tazobactam (usual 3.375 g every 6 hours): above 40: no change; 20 to 40: 2.25 g every 6 hours; below 20: 2.25 g every 8 hours; haemodialysis: 2.25 g every 12 hours plus 0.75 g after each session. For the 4.5 g pneumonia regimen: 20 to 40: 3.375 g every 6 hours; below 20: 2.25 g every 6 hours; haemodialysis: 2.25 g every 8 hours plus 0.75 g after each session.

sections.title: Cephalosporins
sections.text:
• Cefazolin: CrCl 55 or above: usual dose; 35 to 54: usual dose at least 8 hours apart; 11 to 34: half the dose every 12 hours; 10 or below: half the dose every 18 to 24 hours.
• Cefalexin: CrCl 15 to 29: 250 mg every 8 to 12 hours; 5 to 14: 250 mg every 24 hours; below 5: 250 mg every 48 to 60 hours.
• Cefuroxime IV: above 20: 750 mg to 1.5 g every 8 hours; 10 to 20: 750 mg every 12 hours; below 10: 750 mg every 24 hours.
• Cefepime (usual 2 g every 8 hours): 30 to 60: 2 g every 12 hours; 11 to 29: 2 g every 24 hours; below 11: 1 g every 24 hours. (usual 2 g every 12 hours: 30 to 60: 2 g every 24 hours; 11 to 29: 1 g every 24 hours; below 11: 500 mg every 24 hours).
• Ceftriaxone: no adjustment for renal impairment alone (maximum 2 g a day in combined severe renal and hepatic failure).
• Ceftazidime and the newer combinations: use the bands in the Drugs tab or your local table; the label bands are for lower doses than are often given for serious infection.

sections.title: Carbapenems and aztreonam
sections.text:
• Meropenem (usual 1 g every 8 hours): CrCl 26 to 50: 1 g every 12 hours; 10 to 25: 500 mg every 12 hours; below 10: 500 mg every 24 hours.
• Ertapenem: CrCl above 30: 1 g every 24 hours; 30 or below, including haemodialysis: 500 mg every 24 hours.
• Imipenem-cilastatin (usual 500 mg every 6 hours): CrCl 60 to 89: 400 mg every 6 hours; 30 to 59: 300 mg every 6 hours; 15 to 29: 200 mg every 6 hours; below 15: avoid unless dialysis is started within 48 hours.
• Aztreonam: CrCl 10 to 30: 50% of the dose after the loading dose; below 10: 25% of the dose after the loading dose.

sections.title: Quinolones, folate antagonists, urinary agents
sections.text:
• Ciprofloxacin: CrCl 30 to 50: 250 to 500 mg every 12 hours; 5 to 29: 250 to 500 mg every 18 hours orally (or 200 to 400 mg IV every 18 to 24 hours).
• Levofloxacin 750 mg every 24 hours: CrCl 20 to 49: 750 mg every 48 hours; 10 to 19 or haemodialysis: 750 mg once, then 500 mg every 48 hours.
• Moxifloxacin: no adjustment.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: CrCl 15 to 30: 50% of the dose; below 15: avoid, or use 50% with close monitoring.
• Nitrofurantoin: avoid when CrCl is below 30 (the label says below 60); urine levels are too low to work.
• Fosfomycin oral single dose: works less well when CrCl is below about 30; IV doses need a protocol.

sections.title: Glycopeptides, aminoglycosides, others
sections.text:
• Vancomycin: dose by levels in all patients with kidney impairment; use a loading dose, then AUC- or trough-guided maintenance (see the TDM tab).
• Gentamicin and amikacin: dose by levels, extend the interval as CrCl falls, and avoid extended-interval dosing when CrCl is below about 40.
• Daptomycin: CrCl below 30, including dialysis: the same dose every 48 hours.
• Colistin: reduce the daily maintenance dose by CrCl, using a validated nomogram; polymyxin B usually needs no kidney adjustment.
• Linezolid: no adjustment, although metabolites accumulate and blood counts need closer monitoring.

sections.title: No adjustment for kidney function
sections.text:
• Azithromycin, clarithromycin (reduce below CrCl 30), doxycycline, minocycline, clindamycin, metronidazole, moxifloxacin, linezolid, tigecycline, rifampicin, nafcillin, oxacillin, flucloxacillin (mild to moderate impairment), fidaxomicin, tedizolid and ceftriaxone.
• Check each drug in the Drugs tab for cautions and interactions.

items.source: Product labelling (as summarised in the Drugs tab), Sanford Guide, BNF renal impairment tables. Verify against the current label and your local pharmacy table.

items.title: Dialysis and CRRT dosing
items.subtitle: Intermittent haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, CRRT
items.summary: For intermittent haemodialysis, give drugs after the session on dialysis days. CRRT clears many antibiotics, so dosing depends on the effluent flow rate. Always use a local table, because practice varies.

sections.title: Intermittent haemodialysis (principles)
sections.text:
• Give doses after the session on dialysis days, so the drug is not removed immediately.
• Highly dialysed: most beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, vancomycin (more with high-flux membranes), metronidazole, fluconazole, ciprofloxacin.
• Little dialysed: azithromycin, doxycycline, clindamycin, ceftriaxone, daptomycin (partly), tigecycline, rifampicin, linezolid (about 30%, give after the session).
• Check pre-dialysis levels for vancomycin and gentamicin to guide the next dose.

sections.title: Haemodialysis examples
sections.text:
• Cefazolin: 2 g after each session, or 2 g, 2 g and 3 g after the three weekly sessions.
• Vancomycin: loading dose 20 to 25 mg/kg, then about 5 to 10 mg/kg after each session, guided by pre-dialysis levels.
• Gentamicin: 1 to 2 mg/kg after each session, guided by pre-dialysis levels.
• Meropenem: 500 mg every 24 hours, given after dialysis on dialysis days.
• Ertapenem: 500 mg every 24 hours; if given within 6 hours before dialysis, give a supplemental 150 mg afterwards.
• Piperacillin-tazobactam: see the bands in the previous entry.

sections.title: Peritoneal dialysis peritonitis
sections.text:
• Follow the ISPD guideline: take cloudy effluent for cell count and culture, and treat early.
• Empirical therapy covers Gram-positives (vancomycin or a first-generation cephalosporin) and Gram-negatives (ceftazidime or cefepime, or an aminoglycoside).
• Intraperitoneal dosing is preferred, with doses given in the ISPD tables for intermittent and continuous regimens, which depend on whether the patient is on continuous ambulatory or automated dialysis.
• Typical duration: 2 weeks, and 3 weeks for severe or complicated infection, S. aureus, enterococci or Pseudomonas.
• Remove the catheter for refractory peritonitis, relapsing infection, fungal infection or tunnel infection.

sections.title: CRRT principles
sections.text:
• Do not reduce the first 24 to 48 hours of beta-lactam doses; give a full loading dose.
• Dose depends on effluent rate (usually 20 to 35 mL/kg/hour), the filter, and residual kidney function.
• Underdosing is a bigger risk than overdosing in the first days, so use extended infusions and therapeutic drug monitoring where available.
• Typical ranges (effluent-dependent): meropenem 1 g every 8 to 12 hours; piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours (or 3.375 g every 6 hours); cefepime 1 to 2 g every 12 hours; ceftriaxone 2 g every 24 hours; ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 12 hours; vancomycin loading dose 15 to 25 mg/kg then level-guided maintenance.
• Gentamicin and amikacin: loading dose, then dose by levels.

sections.title: Practical advice
sections.text:
• Pharmacy and infectious diseases review is strongly advised for every patient on CRRT.
• Reassess doses when the effluent rate, filter or renal replacement mode changes, or when residual renal function recovers.
• Document the dialysis schedule and the dosing assumptions on the prescription.
• These ranges are indicative only: use your local CRRT dosing table.

items.source: SCCM/ASHP critical care dosing guidance, ISPD 2022 peritonitis guidance, product labelling. Indicative ranges only: verify against your local CRRT and dialysis tables.

items.title: Dosing in obesity
items.subtitle: Adults | BMI 30 or above
items.summary: Volume of distribution rises in obesity, but organ clearance does not rise as much. Use actual, ideal or adjusted weight depending on the drug, and monitor levels for vancomycin and aminoglycosides.

sections.title: Weights
sections.text:
• Ideal body weight (IBW): men 50 kg + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 feet; women 45.5 kg + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 feet.
• Adjusted body weight = IBW + 0.4 x (actual weight minus IBW).
• Body mass index of 30 or more counts as obesity; severe obesity above 40.
• Do not cap weight-based doses without a reason, and do not reduce initial doses of time-critical antibiotics.

sections.title: Beta-lactams
sections.text:
• Fixed standard doses are usually appropriate, but consider the higher end of the range in severe infection.
• Cefazolin prophylaxis: 2 g, or 3 g if the patient weighs 120 kg or more.
• Piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem: extended infusions help achieve targets; follow local protocol.
• Ceftriaxone: 2 g once a day is often used for serious infection, with no further weight adjustment.

sections.title: Glycopeptides and aminoglycosides
sections.text:
• Vancomycin: loading dose 20 to 35 mg/kg of actual body weight (usually capped at 3 g), then level-guided maintenance (see the TDM tab).
• Gentamicin and tobramycin: use adjusted body weight (IBW + 0.4 x excess).
• Amikacin: adjusted body weight, with levels.
• Monitor creatinine and levels, because overdosing causes toxicity.

sections.title: Other antibiotics
sections.text:
• Daptomycin: actual body weight is used by many protocols, with others using adjusted weight; check local policy.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (weight-based): adjusted body weight.
• Fixed-dose drugs (linezolid, azithromycin, doxycycline, clindamycin 600 to 900 mg, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, rifampicin): no weight adjustment is needed.
• Colistin and polymyxin B: follow the consensus guidelines in the Drugs tab.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Data are limited for many antibiotics in morbid obesity: use therapeutic drug monitoring where available.
• Check renal function using an appropriate weight (see the kidney function entry).
• Review the dose again if the patient loses or gains weight significantly.

items.source: IDSA/ASHP guidance and published pharmacokinetic reviews of antibiotic dosing in obesity. Verify against local protocols.

items.title: Antibiotics in liver impairment
items.subtitle: Adults | Child-Pugh A, B and C
items.summary: Few antibiotics need dose changes for liver disease, but several should be avoided or reduced in severe impairment, and some are hepatotoxic. Monitor liver tests during long courses.

sections.title: Reduce the dose or use caution
sections.text:
• Tigecycline: in severe impairment (Child-Pugh C), give 100 mg, then 25 mg every 12 hours.
• Metronidazole: reduce the dose by about 50% in Child-Pugh C.
• Rifampicin and isoniazid: use cautiously, with close liver monitoring; avoid in severe liver disease where possible.
• Clindamycin and erythromycin: use caution; avoid erythromycin estolate.
• Ceftriaxone: do not exceed 2 g a day when there is combined severe hepatic and renal failure.
• Fluoroquinolones: moxifloxacin is not recommended in Child-Pugh C.

sections.title: Hepatotoxic antibiotics to use with care
sections.text:
• Flucloxacillin: cholestatic hepatitis, sometimes weeks after stopping.
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate: cholestatic hepatitis, more often in older men and after courses over 14 days.
• Nitrofurantoin: hepatitis in long-term use.
• Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide: hepatitis, so check liver tests regularly.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: rare severe hepatitis.
• Tigecycline: raised liver enzymes; and daptomycin, linezolid and ceftaroline can raise liver enzymes on long courses.

sections.title: Generally safe, no adjustment
sections.text:
• Most beta-lactams (penicillin, ampicillin, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefazolin, cefepime, carbapenems), vancomycin, aminoglycosides, fosfomycin, and colistin are cleared by the kidney, so liver disease alone does not require a change.
• Remember that cirrhosis with hepatorenal syndrome changes renal clearance.

sections.title: Cirrhosis and ascites
sections.text:
• Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: ceftriaxone 2 g once a day for 5 days, plus albumin on days 1 and 3.
• Prophylaxis after an episode: ciprofloxacin 500 mg once a day, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet once a day.
• Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, vancomycin at high troughs) in cirrhosis, because of the risk of hepatorenal syndrome.
• Avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins.

sections.title: Monitoring
sections.text:
• Check liver tests at baseline and weekly for long courses of hepatotoxic drugs.
• Stop the drug and seek advice for jaundice, rising transaminases above 3 times the upper limit with symptoms, or above 5 times without symptoms.
• Review other hepatotoxic medicines, alcohol and paracetamol use.

items.source: Product labelling (as summarised in the Drugs tab), AASLD guidance on ascites and SBP. Verify against the current label.

items.title: Paediatric dosing principles
items.subtitle: Children beyond the neonatal period
items.summary: Dose by actual body weight, cap at the adult dose, and check the concentration of every suspension. Several adult antibiotics are restricted in children. Neonates need a separate formulary.

sections.title: Basics
sections.text:
• Use current actual weight in kg; for obese children use ideal or adjusted weight and cap at the adult dose.
• Never exceed the adult maximum dose, even if the weight-based dose would be higher.
• Write doses as mg/kg per dose and per day, and state the interval; confusion between the two is a common cause of error.
• Check the strength of each liquid (mg per 5 mL) before prescribing and when dispensing.
• Round to a measurable volume, and use an oral syringe rather than a spoon.

sections.title: Renal and hepatic function
sections.text:
• Kidney function matures through the first year of life: dose intervals are longer in preterm and young infants.
• Use the Schwartz equation for children: eGFR = 0.413 x height (cm) / serum creatinine (mg/dL).
• Adjust the interval for impaired kidney function as in the adult renal bands, scaled to the paediatric dose.
• Monitor levels for gentamicin, amikacin and vancomycin.

sections.title: Drugs restricted in children
sections.text:
• Tetracyclines: avoid under 8 years, except when no alternative exists or for serious infection such as rickettsial disease and anthrax; short courses of doxycycline carry little risk of tooth staining.
• Fluoroquinolones: avoid unless benefits outweigh risks, for example multidrug-resistant infection, cystic fibrosis, anthrax and plague.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: avoid under 2 months of age (kernicterus).
• Chloramphenicol: avoid in neonates (grey baby syndrome).
• Ceftriaxone: avoid in neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia or receiving IV calcium.
• Clindamycin and erythromycin: watch for diarrhoea and C. difficile; erythromycin and azithromycin carry a risk of pyloric stenosis in the first weeks of life.

sections.title: Practical points
sections.text:
• Oral first-line is amoxicillin for most community infections; use the high-dose form for pneumococcal disease.
• Switch from IV to oral as soon as the child is improving and feeding.
• Duration is often shorter than in adults: for example 5 days for community-acquired pneumonia and 5 to 10 days for otitis media, depending on age.
• Taste and palatability affect adherence: flucloxacillin, clindamycin and some macrolides are poorly tolerated.
• Provide written instructions and advise on completing the course.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• The entries that follow list common antibiotic doses by weight, grouped by oral and IV route.
• Neonatal dosing depends on gestational and postnatal age: use your neonatal formulary, not this tab.
• See the Drugs tab for adult monographs and cautions.

items.source: BNF for Children, AAP Red Book, Harriet Lane Handbook and IDSA paediatric guidance. Doses are for children beyond the neonatal period; never exceed the adult dose; verify against the current formulary and local protocol.

items.title: Paediatric oral antibiotic doses
items.subtitle: Children 1 month and older | mg/kg, capped at the adult dose
items.summary: Doses by weight for the commonly used oral antibiotics. Always check the suspension strength and the maximum dose.

sections.title: Penicillins and cephalosporins
sections.text:
• Amoxicillin: 25 to 50 mg/kg/day divided every 8 to 12 hours; high dose 80 to 90 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours for otitis media, sinusitis and pneumococcal pneumonia (maximum 4 g a day).
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate: 25 to 45 mg/kg/day (amoxicillin component) divided every 12 hours; for 90 mg/kg/day use the 14:1 (extra-strength) formulation to keep clavulanate at or below 10 mg/kg/day.
• Penicillin V: 25 to 50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours; for streptococcal pharyngitis 250 mg every 12 hours if 27 kg or less, or 500 mg every 12 hours if above 27 kg, for 10 days.
• Cefalexin: 25 to 50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (up to 100 mg/kg/day in serious infection; maximum 4 g a day).
• Cefuroxime axetil: 20 to 30 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours (maximum 1 g a day).
• Cefpodoxime: 10 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours (maximum 400 mg a day).
• Cefixime: 8 mg/kg/day once a day or divided every 12 hours (maximum 400 mg a day).
• Cefdinir: 14 mg/kg/day once a day or divided every 12 hours (maximum 600 mg a day).

sections.title: Macrolides and lincosamides
sections.text:
• Azithromycin (pneumonia and otitis media): 10 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) on day 1, then 5 mg/kg (maximum 250 mg) once a day on days 2 to 5.
• Azithromycin (streptococcal pharyngitis): 12 mg/kg once a day for 5 days (maximum 500 mg).
• Azithromycin (pertussis): 10 mg/kg once a day for 5 days; under 1 month, 10 mg/kg once a day for 5 days with monitoring for pyloric stenosis.
• Clarithromycin: 15 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours (maximum 1 g a day).
• Clindamycin: 10 to 30 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 1.8 g a day).

sections.title: Other oral agents
sections.text:
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: 8 to 12 mg/kg/day of trimethoprim divided every 12 hours (cystitis, MRSA skin infection); not under 2 months.
• Metronidazole: 30 to 40 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 4 g a day); for giardiasis 15 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours for 5 to 7 days.
• Doxycycline (8 years and older, or when needed for serious infection at any age): 2 to 4 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours (maximum 200 mg a day); children 45 kg and over receive the adult dose.
• Nitrofurantoin (not under 1 month): 5 to 7 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours (maximum 400 mg a day).
• Linezolid: under 12 years 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (maximum 600 mg per dose); 12 years and older 600 mg every 12 hours.
• Ciprofloxacin (only when benefits outweigh risks): 20 to 30 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours (maximum 1.5 g a day).

sections.title: Prophylaxis and special doses
sections.text:
• Rifampicin for meningococcal contacts: 10 mg/kg every 12 hours for 2 days (5 mg/kg for infants under 1 month), maximum 600 mg per dose.
• Rifampicin for Hib contacts: 20 mg/kg once a day for 4 days (maximum 600 mg).
• Penicillin V prophylaxis after splenectomy or in sickle cell disease: 125 mg twice a day for children under 5, and 250 mg twice a day from 5 years; follow local policy.
• Rheumatic fever secondary prophylaxis: penicillin V 250 mg twice a day, or benzathine penicillin G IM every 3 to 4 weeks.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Bioavailability and palatability matter: follow the child's age and local formulary.
• Always cap at the adult dose, and check the maximum for each drug.
• See the Drugs tab for monographs, interactions and cautions.

items.source: BNF for Children, AAP Red Book, Harriet Lane Handbook and IDSA paediatric guidance. Doses are for children beyond the neonatal period; never exceed the adult dose; verify against the current formulary and local protocol.

items.title: Paediatric IV beta-lactam doses
items.subtitle: Children 1 month and older | mg/kg, capped at the adult dose
items.summary: IV penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and aztreonam by weight, with the higher doses used for meningitis. Check the maximum daily dose for each.

sections.title: Penicillins
sections.text:
• Penicillin G: 100,000 to 250,000 units/kg/day divided every 4 to 6 hours; meningitis 250,000 to 400,000 units/kg/day (maximum 24 million units a day).
• Ampicillin: 100 to 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours; meningitis 300 to 400 mg/kg/day (maximum 12 g a day).
• Flucloxacillin, nafcillin or oxacillin: 100 to 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours (maximum 12 g a day).
• Piperacillin-tazobactam: 240 to 300 mg/kg/day of the piperacillin component divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 16 g a day of piperacillin).

sections.title: Cephalosporins
sections.text:
• Cefazolin: 50 to 100 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 6 g a day); surgical prophylaxis 30 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) within 60 minutes before incision.
• Cefuroxime: 100 to 150 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 6 g a day).
• Ceftriaxone: 50 to 75 mg/kg once a day (maximum 2 g); meningitis 100 mg/kg/day once a day or divided every 12 hours (maximum 4 g a day); avoid in neonates.
• Cefotaxime: 150 to 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours; meningitis 225 to 300 mg/kg/day (maximum 12 g a day).
• Ceftazidime: 150 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 6 g a day).
• Cefepime: 150 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 6 g a day); 100 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours for milder infection.

sections.title: Carbapenems and aztreonam
sections.text:
• Meropenem: 60 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 3 g a day); meningitis 120 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (maximum 6 g a day).
• Ertapenem: 3 months to 12 years, 15 mg/kg every 12 hours (maximum 1 g a day); 13 years and older, 1 g once a day.
• Aztreonam: 90 to 120 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 8 g a day).

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Extended infusions of beta-lactams are used in some paediatric intensive care units: follow your unit protocol.
• Renal impairment: lengthen the interval as in the adult bands.
• For neonates use the neonatal formulary.

items.source: BNF for Children, AAP Red Book, Harriet Lane Handbook and IDSA paediatric guidance. Doses are for children beyond the neonatal period; never exceed the adult dose; verify against the current formulary and local protocol.

items.title: Paediatric IV doses: glycopeptides, aminoglycosides and others
items.subtitle: Children 1 month and older | mg/kg, with level monitoring
items.summary: Vancomycin and aminoglycosides need level-guided dosing. Clindamycin, metronidazole, linezolid, azithromycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole have weight-based IV doses.

sections.title: Vancomycin
sections.text:
• Usual: 40 to 60 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours.
• Serious MRSA infection: 60 to 80 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours, adjusted to levels.
• Target an AUC/MIC of 400 to 600 where AUC monitoring is available (see the TDM tab); trough-only targets are no longer preferred.
• A loading dose of 20 to 25 mg/kg is used by some protocols in critically ill children.
• Monitor creatinine, and avoid combining with other nephrotoxins where possible.

sections.title: Aminoglycosides
sections.text:
• Gentamicin: 5 to 7.5 mg/kg/day given once a day or divided every 8 hours; dose by levels.
• Amikacin: 15 to 20 mg/kg once a day, with levels.
• Monitor creatinine, and check hearing in long courses and in cystic fibrosis.
• Neonatal dosing is by gestational age: use the neonatal formulary.

sections.title: Other IV agents
sections.text:
• Clindamycin: 25 to 40 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 2.7 g a day).
• Metronidazole: 30 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 4 g a day).
• Linezolid: under 12 years 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (maximum 600 mg per dose); 12 years and older 600 mg every 12 hours.
• Azithromycin IV: 10 mg/kg once a day (maximum 500 mg).
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole IV: 8 to 12 mg/kg/day of trimethoprim divided every 6 to 12 hours; for Pneumocystis pneumonia 15 to 20 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours.
• Acyclovir and antifungals have separate dosing: not included here.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Always confirm doses with the unit pharmacist or a paediatric formulary for children who are very small, critically ill or have kidney disease.
• See the Drugs tab for monographs on vancomycin, gentamicin, amikacin, clindamycin and linezolid.

items.source: BNF for Children, AAP Red Book, Harriet Lane Handbook and IDSA paediatric guidance. Doses are for children beyond the neonatal period; never exceed the adult dose; verify against the current formulary and local protocol.

items.title: Neonatal infection: empirical regimens and cautions
items.subtitle: Neonates | gestational age and postnatal age determine dose
items.summary: This entry lists empirical drug choices and cautions only. Neonatal doses and intervals depend on gestational age, postnatal age and weight, so use your neonatal formulary.

sections.title: Early-onset sepsis (first 72 hours)
sections.text:
• Usual organisms: group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria.
• Empirical therapy: ampicillin plus gentamicin.
• Add cefotaxime where Gram-negative meningitis is suspected.
• Treat for at least 7 days for culture-positive sepsis and 14 to 21 days for meningitis depending on the organism.
• Stop antibiotics at 36 to 48 hours if cultures are negative and the baby is well, per local policy.

sections.title: Late-onset sepsis
sections.text:
• Common organisms: coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Gram-negative bacilli, and Candida.
• Empirical therapy: flucloxacillin or vancomycin, plus gentamicin or cefotaxime, according to local resistance.
• Healthcare-associated infection with risk of resistant Gram-negatives: a carbapenem may be needed, with specialist advice.
• Remove infected central lines when possible.

sections.title: Meningitis
sections.text:
• Cefotaxime plus ampicillin (to cover Listeria), with or without gentamicin; add aciclovir when herpes simplex virus is suspected.
• Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates.
• Lumbar puncture when the baby is stable, and repeat the CSF when the organism is Gram-negative.

sections.title: Drugs to avoid or use with caution
sections.text:
• Ceftriaxone: contraindicated with IV calcium and in neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia.
• Chloramphenicol: grey baby syndrome.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and other sulfonamides: kernicterus risk.
• Fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines: avoid unless there is no alternative.
• Erythromycin and azithromycin: risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
• Gentamicin and vancomycin: monitor levels and kidney function.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Neonatal drug clearance changes rapidly in the first weeks: dose intervals lengthen with prematurity.
• Follow your neonatal unit formulary, such as the BNFc neonatal section or your hospital protocol.
• This entry is not a dosing source for neonates.

items.source: BNF for Children (neonatal), NICE neonatal infection guideline, AAP Red Book. Use your neonatal formulary for all doses.

items.title: Antibiotics in pregnancy
items.subtitle: Quick reference by drug class
items.summary: Penicillins, cephalosporins, clindamycin, metronidazole, azithromycin and fosfomycin are generally acceptable. Avoid tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the first trimester and at term, unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.

sections.title: Generally acceptable
sections.text:
• Penicillins (penicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin), cephalosporins, and carbapenems when needed.
• Azithromycin and erythromycin base (avoid erythromycin estolate).
• Clindamycin and metronidazole (including in the first trimester when needed).
• Vancomycin, fosfomycin and cefalexin for urinary infection.
• Nitrofurantoin: acceptable in the first and second trimester when there is no better choice; avoid near term and in labour.

sections.title: Use only when the benefit outweighs the risk
sections.text:
• Aminoglycosides: short courses for serious infection with level monitoring; streptomycin and kanamycin carry the highest risk of fetal ototoxicity.
• Clarithromycin: prefer azithromycin.
• Rifampicin: used for tuberculosis; give vitamin K to the newborn if used near term.
• Linezolid, daptomycin, newer beta-lactam combinations: limited data, specialist advice.
• Isoniazid and ethambutol are used in pregnancy for tuberculosis, with pyridoxine for isoniazid.

sections.title: Avoid
sections.text:
• Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline): fetal teeth and bone effects, and maternal liver toxicity; exceptions are serious infections such as rickettsial disease and anthrax.
• Fluoroquinolones: avoid unless no safer option exists.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: avoid in the first trimester (folate antagonism) and near term (kernicterus); give folic acid if used.
• Chloramphenicol near term (grey baby syndrome).
• Prolonged high-dose treatments need specialist advice.

sections.title: Common infections in pregnancy
sections.text:
• Asymptomatic bacteriuria and cystitis: treat; cefalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate or fosfomycin, guided by culture.
• Pyelonephritis: admit and give IV ceftriaxone; avoid fluoroquinolones.
• Group B streptococcus in labour: penicillin G or ampicillin; cefazolin if low-risk penicillin allergy.
• Syphilis: benzathine penicillin G only; desensitise if allergic.
• Chlamydia: azithromycin 1 g single dose; Listeria: ampicillin with gentamicin.
• Community-acquired pneumonia: a beta-lactam plus azithromycin.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Check each drug in the Drugs tab, and use pregnancy registries or your pharmacy service for uncommon drugs.
• Infection is also risky for mother and fetus: do not withhold necessary antibiotics because of pregnancy.

items.source: Product labelling (as summarised in the Drugs tab), ACOG and RCOG guidance, CDC STI treatment guidelines. Verify against current guidance.

items.title: Antibiotics and breastfeeding
items.subtitle: Quick reference by drug class
items.summary: Most antibiotics reach milk in very small amounts and are compatible with breastfeeding. Watch the infant for diarrhoea, thrush and rash, and avoid a few drugs in newborns, jaundiced infants and G6PD deficiency.

sections.title: Generally compatible
sections.text:
• Penicillins, cephalosporins, aztreonam and carbapenems.
• Aminoglycosides and vancomycin: poor oral absorption in the infant.
• Azithromycin, erythromycin and clarithromycin: watch for infant diarrhoea; avoid erythromycin in infants under 2 weeks where possible because of pyloric stenosis.
• Clindamycin: watch for diarrhoea or blood in the infant's stool.
• Fosfomycin and rifampicin: acceptable.

sections.title: Use with caution
sections.text:
• Metronidazole: avoid high or prolonged doses; for a single 2 g dose some guidance suggests pausing breastfeeding for 12 to 24 hours.
• Fluoroquinolones: short courses are generally acceptable, with infant monitoring.
• Doxycycline and other tetracyclines: short courses are acceptable; avoid prolonged use.
• Nitrofurantoin: avoid in infants under 1 month and in G6PD deficiency.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: avoid in infants under 2 months, jaundiced or premature infants, and G6PD deficiency.
• Linezolid: limited data; prefer alternatives where possible.

sections.title: Avoid or seek specialist advice
sections.text:
• Chloramphenicol: avoid.
• Tigecycline: limited data.
• Prolonged high-dose therapy: ask a pharmacist or use a lactation database.
• Newer agents (cefiderocol, sulbactam-durlobactam, dalbavancin): limited data.

sections.title: Monitoring the infant
sections.text:
• Diarrhoea, thrush, rash, poor feeding and irritability can follow maternal antibiotics.
• Closer monitoring for premature infants, newborns under 1 month, and infants with jaundice or G6PD deficiency.
• Breastfeeding is rarely a reason to stop a needed antibiotic.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text:
• Your app also holds a LactMed dataset (the NIH drug and lactation database): use it for drugs not covered here.
• Check each drug in the Drugs tab for its pregnancy and lactation summary.

items.source: LactMed (NIH), product labelling (as summarised in the Drugs tab), WHO guidance. Verify against LactMed and a lactation pharmacist for uncommon drugs.
